definition: Contents of consciousness are the distinguishable mental items that make up conscious experience. In the source, they are the kinds of contents that can become linked through experience, so that the return of one tends to bring back another.

provenance.revision: 1901 New York Macmillan original; archive index checked 2026-10-18
provenance.scope: Source record Association (of ideas); pinned source text

reasons: The packet does not define the term “contents of consciousness.” It defines “Association (of ideas)” as a union between mental dispositions corresponding to “two or more distinguishable contents of consciousness,” but it does not give a standalone definition of what “contents of consciousness” are.
The definition’s first sentence (“distinguishable mental items that make up conscious experience”) is not stated in the provided packet.

The definition’s second sentence adds that the contents are “kinds of contents that can become linked through experience” such that “the return of one tends to bring back another.” While a similar idea appears in the packet’s description of association (when one content recurs, the other tends to recur), the packet links this explicitly to “association of ideas,” not to a general definition of “contents of consciousness.”

The source defines association between mental dispositions corresponding to distinguishable contents of consciousness; it does not define the contents themselves as the items that become linked through experience.
The phrase 'make up conscious experience' is an unsupported paraphrase not stated in the packet and is broader than the source text.
